meta.description: Retries post-turn work that failed every inline attempt or was orphaned by a container restart (app/services/task_queue.py). Costs nothing on a healthy system: the queue is drained inline after every turn, so this normally claims zero jobs and returns immediately. It is the third of the three drains — inline, on startup, and here — and the only one that runs when nobody is talking to Igor.

nodes.name: Hourly at :20
nodes.notes:
Hourly, offset to :20 so it does not land on the same minute as the briefings (:00) or Orion's audit (04:00) and queue behind them.

Hourly rather than every few minutes because the queue's own backoff is measured in minutes (2, 15, 60): a job that just failed is not due yet, so checking more often only costs HTTP calls. Hourly rather than daily because a failed session title should be recoverable the same afternoon, not tomorrow.

This is a plain HTTP call with no model behind it — the cheap-probe rule (README) is satisfied: the poll is free, and only a job that actually needs running spends anything.

nodes.name: Igor: drain job queue
nodes.notes:
Returns {claimed, succeeded, failed, reclaimed, queue:{...}} — an empty claim is the healthy result, not silence.

Watch `queue.failed`. A job reaches that state only after exhausting every retry, so a non-zero count is a real bug someone has to look at, not a transient. It never clears itself: `failed` is terminal by design, because a job that silently un-fails would hide the fault that caused it.

Only X-API-Key here, not X-N8N-Secret — /admin endpoints take the API key alone (the double-header rule covers the /trigger and probe surfaces, which read owner data). Matches the existing DELETE /admin/outputs workflow.

The 2-minute timeout covers a backlog whose handlers make LLM calls. If it times out the jobs stay claimed and the next sweep's reclaim pass recovers them — nothing is lost by a slow drain.
